title: Verifier‑Grounded Evaluation of LLM‑Generated Network Configurations: A Preregistered NetConfig‑Semantic Study (estimand: verifier‑consistency under identical inputs)
abstract: We report a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; preregistration SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) that evaluated a deterministic template baseline versus a single‑pass LLM generator (declared_model_version = gpt‑5‑mini) on N = 120 synthetic intent→configuration tasks using a deterministic validator. Crucially, the preregistered estimand tested by the confirmatory analysis is verifier‑consistency under identical inputs (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate"). Under these frozen semantics every confirmatory episode completed: baseline = 120/120 verifier passes; guarded (gpt‑5‑mini, shared seed_0) = 120/120 verifier passes. Paired difference = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); McNemar exact two‑sided p = 1.0. We publish the complete execution and analysis artifacts and per‑file SHA‑256 fingerprints required for byte‑for‑byte reproduction (see execution/execution_manifest.json in the artifact bundle). We diagnose—using the archived traces—why the preregistered shared_initial_candidate design produced a degenerate paired outcome (identical canonical candidate per pair + deterministic validator) and provide artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory design, validator diversification, and expanded task heterogeneity) that convert the experiment into an operationally informative test of independent generative reliability while preserving reproducibility. The immutable initial master prompt is archived (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

sections.introduction: Translating operator intent into device configuration is a core NetOps task where correctness is safety‑critical: incorrect commands can break reachability, violate ACLs, or create unsafe transient states during multi‑step changes. Offline deterministic validators (reachability/ACL/routing analyzers in the Batfish lineage) are commonly used to audit configuration artifacts pre‑deployment [https://doi.org/10.1145/3603269.3604866]. Large language models (LLMs) promise rapid intent→config generation but raise operational questions about reliability: operators often need the independent probability that an LLM, when sampled in deployment, will produce a verifier‑passing configuration. Our preregistered confirmatory estimand differs: it asks whether a deterministic verifier treats identical candidate artifacts differently across two scoring conditions (verifier‑consistency under identical inputs). This paper (i) publishes an exhaustive artifact bundle that allows byte‑for‑byte reproduction of the run and its exact inputs/outputs, (ii) reports the preregistered confirmatory outcome (baseline = 120/120, guarded = 120/120; paired diff = 0.00; 95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0) with archival pointers to the exact validator traces that produced those numbers, and (iii) provides artifact‑grounded, immediately runnable experiment modifications that answer the operational question practitioners typically want (independent_per_condition generative reliability).
sections.related_work: Verifier‑grounded evaluation and generate–validate–repair. Deterministic configuration verifiers (Batfish and related tools) provide operationally meaningful, auditable pass/fail judgments on static configs and are now standard for pre‑deployment validation [Brown et al., 2023; doi:10.1145/3603269.3604866]. LLM→NetOps literature generally explores generate–validate–repair pipelines, iteration budgets, and sampling semantics (single‑pass vs multi‑seed vs bounded repair) with results showing that orchestration and feedback often dominate raw model choice for repair effectiveness (see iterative‑repair analyses in the evidence bundle). Two methodological axes matter: (A) sampling semantics—shared canonical candidate vs independent per‑condition draws; (B) validator scope—syntactic parsing vs transient safety checks vs multi‑verifier ensembles. Our study intentionally froze sampling semantics (shared_initial_candidate) to test a distinct estimand (validator response reproducibility), a design choice we make explicit here to avoid conflation with independent generative reliability studies. We also publish per‑episode validator traces so readers can verify how the validator enforced task‑encoded workflow_policies (example traces: execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1add7c5a57f...).
sections.methodology: Preregistration and frozen plan. The study preregistration (CAND‑2026‑001‑NetConfig‑Semantic‑v1; SHA‑256 7db1663cf3982c8ea1e16c3dd7c0348f356bb4cbe3978ecc75bb59fdedb71a37) specified a paired design across N = 120 programmatic tasks (40 per topology class), primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, confirmatory generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate", validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator_version 5.0), and the exact analysis plan (paired_binary_analysis_v1) including bootstrap parameters (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Tasks were synthesized from a deterministic template bank (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5, v5.0). Each task manifest encodes initial_state, expected_final_state, required_sequence, workflow_policies (e.g., must_be_down_for_fields, minimum_active_in_groups), allowed_touched_fields, and difficulty metadata; representative manifests and their SHA‑256s appear in execution/task_manifest.jsonl (see artifact_examples).

Representative validator traces show parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, and validation_after.valid = true for canonical candidates (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 0d56c1add7c5a57f...).
sections.discussion: Why the confirmatory contingency is degenerate — artifact‑visible causal chain. The confirmatory estimand was verifier‑consistency under identical inputs; the preregistered shared_initial_candidate design generated a single canonical LLM candidate per task and reused it for both baseline and guarded scoring episodes. A deterministic validator necessarily returns the same binary outcome for identical inputs; the archived candidate files (execution/responses/*-shared-initial.txt; representative SHA‑256s: task-000001 8f38c8be..., task-000002 ae967f70..., task-000003 f7f4db24...) combined with the per‑episode validator JSON traces explain the degenerate paired table (n_11 = 120). This is an intended, auditable result for the preregistered estimand but does not estimate independent generative reliability.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, verifier‑grounded paired experiment and released exhaustive artifacts enabling exact reproduction (execution/execution_manifest.json and per‑file SHA‑256). Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics both deterministic template baseline and gpt‑5‑mini guarded condition passed the deterministic validator on all N = 120 tasks (120/120 each). Archived evidence demonstrates that identical canonical candidates per pair combined with deterministic validator behavior caused the degenerate paired outcome; therefore the confirmatory result does not speak to independent per‑condition generative reliability in deployment. We provide artifact‑grounded, runnable modifications (independent_per_condition sampling, multi‑seed confirmatory design, validator diversification, and expanded task heterogeneity) and point to exact artifact locations to enable deterministic reruns that answer the operational question NetOps practitioners require. Full artifact manifest and SHA‑256 fingerprints are published to enable external audit; the immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

limitations: Controlled synthetic tasks: programmatic templates produce narrow required_sequences and workflow_policies that favour canonical solutions and limit external generalizability to heterogeneous operational intents.

Confirmatory shared_initial semantics: the preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' supplied identical canonical candidates to both conditions per pair, removing generation variance and causing the degenerate paired outcome.

Single canonical seed for the confirmatory test: the primary analysis used one canonical seed per task; preregistered exploratory multi‑seed analyses (seeds_1..4) exist in the artifact bundle but were not part of the primary confirmatory inference reported here.

Validator–task coupling: the deterministic validator enforces constraints encoded in the task templates which can increase pass rates for template‑aligned candidates and reduce construct validity for open distributions.

Possible training‑data exposure: preregistered contamination heuristics found no flags under the chosen thresholds, but absence of a heuristic flag is not proof of zero exposure to related artifacts in model pretraining.

Single‑model, single‑validator run: results apply only to gpt‑5‑mini under the recorded configuration and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; they do not generalize across model families, agentic pipelines, or other validators.
